reference.source: Movement-disorder and neurogenetics textbooks with peer-reviewed reviews
clinicalPearls: Primary familial brain calcification (Fahr disease) is a genetic disorder of symmetrical brain calcification, most commonly autosomal dominant through variants in SLC20A2, PDGFB, PDGFRB, or XPR1 (recessive genes also described)
Diagnosis requires exclusion of secondary causes of basal ganglia calcification, above all disorders of calcium-phosphate metabolism such as hypoparathyroidism and pseudohypoparathyroidism

Clinical features are variable and include a movement disorder (parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea), cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms, headache, and seizures, though some carriers remain asymptomatic

CT is the most sensitive means of demonstrating the calcification, showing symmetrical dense deposits in the basal ganglia (especially globus pallidus), thalamus, dentate nuclei, and subcortical white matter
On MRI the calcification can be missed or appear variable, so CT is preferred for detection and characterisation
Serum calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone must be checked to exclude the important treatable metabolic mimics
Because inheritance is often dominant, family history and consideration of testing relatives are important
Management is symptomatic, and calcium-phosphate homeostasis should be optimised where relevant
reference.pathophysiology: Primary familial brain calcification is characterised by progressive bilateral calcium deposition in the basal ganglia and other deep brain structures in the absence of a metabolic cause. The recognised genes converge on the neurovascular unit and phosphate homeostasis: SLC20A2 and XPR1 regulate inorganic phosphate transport, while PDGFB and PDGFRB maintain pericyte function and blood-brain barrier integrity. Disruption of phosphate handling and of the barrier is thought to promote mineral deposition within and around small vessel walls, leading to the calcification that underlies the movement, cognitive, and psychiatric manifestations.
additionalDifferentials: Other endocrine or metabolic causes of brain calcification
Congenital or acquired infections with intracranial calcification
Mitochondrial disorders and other neurodegenerative parkinsonism/dementia syndromes
Toxic causes (for example prior radiation or lead exposure)
Physiological age-related pallidal calcification (as a benign incidental finding)
additionalInvestigations: Brain CT to demonstrate and characterise the symmetrical deep grey-matter and dentate calcification
Serum calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone to exclude parathyroid and metabolic causes
Molecular genetic testing of the known primary familial brain calcification genes
Brain MRI to assess associated parenchymal change and complement CT
Screening for secondary causes (infective and toxic) when the picture is atypical
redFlags: Rapidly progressive cognitive decline or acute psychiatric crisis
Features suggesting a treatable metabolic cause such as symptomatic hypocalcaemia
reference.prognosis: The course is variable: some gene carriers remain asymptomatic while others develop progressive movement disorder, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disease, and there is no treatment that halts the calcification. Prognosis depends on the extent and rate of neurological involvement.
pitfalls: Diagnosing primary (genetic) disease without first excluding secondary metabolic causes, particularly parathyroid disorders
Relying on MRI, which can under-detect calcification, rather than CT
Interpreting minor age-related pallidal calcification as pathological
Overlooking dominant inheritance and the value of family assessment and counselling
management: No therapy halts the calcification, so management is symptomatic and supportive
Symptomatic treatment of the movement disorder, using levodopa or other agents for parkinsonism and appropriate drugs for chorea or dystonia
Psychiatric treatment of associated mood, psychotic or behavioural symptoms alongside cognitive support
Exclusion and correction of secondary metabolic causes, particularly disordered calcium and phosphate handling and hypoparathyroidism, which are important treatable mimics
Multidisciplinary care with neurology, psychiatry and physiotherapy or occupational therapy
Genetic counselling and family assessment given the usually autosomal dominant inheritance
